title: basic driving skills
objectives: Explain safe following-distance rules for different commercial vehicle types and various techniques for driving safely in traffic
Define the term danger zone and describe how to reduce the size of your danger zone
Identify the factors that affect your vehicle's turning characteristics, including off track, and techniques to help you turn safely
Describe how to back up safely, with and without a guide
State when and how to shift gears, including double-clutching and progressive shifting
Identify potential vehicle and personal safety issues and describe how to reduce risks for yourself and other road users

sections.title: Sharing the road
points: Use the two-second rule in a taxi, limousine, ride-hailing vehicle, ambulance or van; leave more space behind motorcycles.
Buses, trucks and other heavy vehicles need at least five seconds; increase it when conditions are less than ideal.
Match the traffic flow within the speed limit; faster or slower than the flow raises your crash risk.
Let tailgaters pass — they may sit in the blind spot directly behind you; keep stops gradual.
Use the right lane when slower than traffic, and four-way flashers driving slowly up or down hills.
Your danger zone is the road you travel before you can stop; it grows with speed and poor roads.
Reduce your danger zone by slowing down and covering the brake pedal when you see a potential hazard.
mustKnow: Two-second following distance: taxi, limousine, ride-hailing vehicle, ambulance or van.
At least five-second following distance: bus, truck or other heavy vehicle.
Leave at least 60 m (200 ft) between large commercial vehicles on a highway.
Vehicles travelling at less than 40 km/h should display a red triangle slow moving vehicle sign.

check.q: What minimum following distance should you keep when driving a bus, truck or other heavy vehicle in ideal conditions?
check.explanation: Heavy vehicles need more time and distance to stop, so keep at least a five-second following distance.

check.q: On a highway, how much space should you leave between your large commercial vehicle and other large commercial vehicles?
check.explanation: The manual says to leave at least 60 m (200 ft) between large commercial vehicles on a highway.

sections.title: Manoeuvring: turns, off track and roundabouts
points: Seat position (conventional, cab-over, forward-control) changes your viewpoint, so you start turns at different points.
Off track: rear wheels follow a different path than front wheels; longer wheelbases and combinations off-track more.
Inertia pushes you off a curve's path — slow down before the curve and apply gradual power through it.
Turning right too tightly can scrape curbs, crowd cyclists, or hit poles; keep your rear close to the curb.
The most dangerous point turning right is when the tractor has turned but the trailer hasn't.
With two left-turn lanes, turn from the right-hand turn lane to accommodate off tracking.
In roundabouts, yield to traffic in the circle; a large vehicle may need more than one lane.
mustKnow: If another vehicle arrives at a traffic circle at the same time as you, yield to the vehicle on your right.
Go around traffic circles and roundabouts to the right (counter-clockwise).
Large trucks and buses may encroach on the median or drive over the truck apron to get through.

choices: The difference between the path of the front wheels and the path of the rear wheels
The distance a vehicle skids when braking hard
The gap between a trailer and the curb during a turn
The turning radius of the steering tires
check.explanation: Off track is the difference between the paths of the front and rear wheels when moving around a curve.

check.q: An intersection has two left-turn lanes. Which lane should you turn from in a large commercial vehicle?
check.explanation: The right-hand turn lane better accommodates your vehicle's off tracking.

sections.title: Backing up
points: With few exceptions, you're responsible for any crash that happens while you're backing up.
Avoid backing up whenever possible; if you must, plan ahead to minimize the distance.
Use a guide whenever possible, positioned with a clear, continuous view and visible to you throughout.
Without a guide, walk completely around the vehicle first and repeat every vehicle length.
Back out of traffic rather than into traffic, and back to the view side, not the blind side.
A series of short backing-up manoeuvres is safer than one long one.
mustKnow: Sound your horn at least once every vehicle length to warn other road users you're about to move.
Without a guide, get out and walk completely around the vehicle before backing; repeat every vehicle length.

check.q: When backing up, how often should you sound your horn?
choices: At least once every vehicle length
Only when someone is visible behind
check.explanation: Sound the horn at least once every vehicle length to warn other road users that you're moving.

sections.title: Seeing and being seen
points: Large vehicles have blind spots in front of the hood, alongside (especially the passenger side) and directly behind.
Scan ahead, behind and to the sides constantly; check mirrors frequently and never assume other drivers see you.
A "stale" green light has been green a while — expect it to change and be prepared to stop.
On freeways, use the far right or centre lane; fewer lane changes means less collision risk.
For emergency vehicles with flashing lights and siren, pull parallel to the nearest edge, stop clear of intersections.
Your air turbulence can endanger cars and cyclists riding near your vehicle; slow down until they're out.
Help drivers pass you safely by reducing speed and giving them room, but don't wave them past.
mustKnow: Passing stopped vehicles with flashing lights: no faster than 70 km/h where the limit is 80 km/h or more.
No faster than 40 km/h where the limit is less than 80 km/h.
If you're in the lane nearest the stopped vehicle, also change lanes if it's safe to do so.
Convex or spot mirrors make things look smaller and farther away than they actually are.

check.q: The speed limit is 100 km/h. How fast may you drive when passing a stopped vehicle displaying flashing lights?
choices: The posted limit, if you change lanes
check.explanation: Where the limit is 80 km/h or more, you must drive no faster than 70 km/h when passing stopped vehicles with flashing lights.

check.q: A small vehicle keeps riding in your area of air turbulence. What should you do?
check.explanation: The manual says to slow down until the smaller vehicle is out of your area of turbulence.

sections.title: Shifting gears and parking
points: Most heavy manual transmissions lack synchromesh gears, so you must become skilled at double-clutching.
Upshifting goes to a higher gear to go faster; downshifting goes lower as you slow down.
Operate between peak torque and peak horsepower — the engine's normal operating r.p.m. range; a tachometer helps.
Shift progressively: use only enough torque to get moving, then shift to the next higher gear.
Before a curve, slow down and downshift to a gear that lets you use engine power throughout.
When parking, set parking brakes, put transmissions in gear (low forward uphill, reverse downhill) and block wheels on grades.
Never use a trailer hand valve to hold an unattended unit — air may drain and release the brakes.
mustKnow: Double-clutching means depressing the clutch pedal twice in the process of moving from one gear to another.
Single-unit vehicle uphill with a curb: turn wheels left toward the centre of the road.
Single-unit vehicle uphill with no curb: turn wheels right toward the edge of the roadway.
Tractor-trailer uphill, with or without a curb: always turn wheels left; on any downgrade, always turn wheels right.
A two-speed axle must be left in low range when parked.

choices: Using two clutch pedals at once
Holding the clutch down through the whole shift
Depressing the clutch pedal twice while moving from one gear to another
check.explanation: Double-clutching is depressing the clutch pedal twice in the process of moving from one gear to another.

check.q: You park a single-unit vehicle facing uphill where there's a curb. Which way do you turn the wheels?
choices: Left, toward the centre of the road
Right, toward the edge of the roadway
It doesn't matter if the parking brake is set
check.explanation: For a single-unit vehicle on an uphill with a curb, turn the wheels left toward the centre of the road.

sections.title: Crossings: intersections and railways
points: Never assume you have the right-of-way; give the right-of-way, don't try to take it.
Get in the proper lane well before turning, signal, and slow gradually; watch for stale green lights.
Don't change lanes, pass or overtake while approaching or going through an intersection.
From an alley, lane or side road, stop before the sidewalk and yield to pedestrians and highway traffic.
At controlled railway crossings, stop when signalled; never cross if the gate is down.
School buses with children, buses with passengers, and vehicles carrying explosive, poisonous or flammable cargo must stop at uncontrolled main crossings.
Never shift gears while crossing railway tracks, and be sure there's room for your vehicle beyond the tracks.
mustKnow: Stop five to 15 m from a railway crossing.
Don't park any vehicle within 15 m of the nearest rail of a railway crossing.
Check the track is clear far enough to give you at least 10 seconds to cross.
The maximum speed in a lane or alley is 20 km/h unless otherwise posted.

check.q: How far from a railway crossing should you stop?
check.explanation: The manual says to stop five to 15 m from the railway crossing.

check.q: What is the maximum speed in a lane or alley unless otherwise posted?
check.explanation: The maximum speed in a lane or alley is 20 km/h unless otherwise posted.

sections.title: Conditions and vehicle safety
points: Watch for animals at dusk and dawn, in spring and fall; if you see one animal, expect more.
If you can't avoid a large animal, brake firmly, steer to strike at an angle, easing off the brake just before impact.
On ice, sleet or snow, test steering and brakes at slow speed, reduce speed and use chains if necessary.
At night, travel at a speed that lets you stop within the distance you can see — high beams light only about 100 m.
Underinflated tires overheat, wear the tread's outer edges and increase hydroplaning risk; check pressure when tires are cool.
Don't drive with loose or missing lug nuts, stripped studs or cracked rims; retorque wheel nuts after changing a tire.
Air- or vacuum-brake vehicles need failure warning devices, and every vehicle needs two braking systems, one mechanical.
mustKnow: Switch from high beam to low beam at least 150 m from any vehicle you're approaching or following.
Defective tire tread: less than 3 mm front or 1.6 mm rear (GVW 5,500 kg or more); less than 1.6 mm on a trailer; less than 3.5 mm for a winter tire.
Tires are defective with tread cuts, cracks or snags longer than 2.5 cm (1 in) deep enough to expose ply cords.
Disabled vehicle: place warning devices approximately 30 m ahead and 30 m behind.
Approved warning devices required for vehicles seating more than 10 passengers or with overall/load width over 2.3 m; daylight flags at least 30 cm by 30 cm.

check.q: On a vehicle with a GVW of 5,500 kg or more, a front tire is defective when its tread depth is less than:
check.explanation: Front tires need at least 3 mm (1/8 in) of tread on vehicles with a GVW of 5,500 kg or more.

check.q: Where should you place warning devices when your commercial vehicle becomes disabled?
choices: About 30 m ahead and 30 m behind
At the vehicle's front and rear bumpers
check.explanation: Place warning devices approximately 30 m ahead and 30 m behind the disabled vehicle.

sections.title: Personal safety
points: Carbon monoxide is odourless, colourless and tasteless; if you feel dizzy or drowsy, pull over and get fresh air.
Wear your seatbelt with the lap belt low over the pelvis and the shoulder strap snug across the chest.
Hand-held electronic devices are prohibited while driving; hands-free single-button devices are permitted for non-GLP drivers.
Alcohol, marijuana, illicit drugs and even some prescribed or stay-awake drugs can impair your driving.
Police can prohibit you if impairment is suspected — no need for BAC over .08 or 2 nanograms THC.
Stay-awake tablets don't reduce mental fatigue; there's no safe substitute for proper rest or sleep.
Never use water on gasoline or oil fires; don't open the hood to fight an under-hood fire.
mustKnow: Correct lap and shoulder belt use reduces the likelihood of death in a crash by 50 per cent; some drivers are exempt at 40 km/h or less.
Allow at least 25 cm (10 in) between your breastbone and the steering-wheel airbag unit.
Police can impound a vehicle for seven days, escalating to 30 or 60 days for repeat offenders; excessive speeding is 40 km/h or more over the limit.
A BC-marked extinguisher puts out grease, oil, gasoline and electrical fires; ABC also puts out Class A fires like paper and cloth.
Vehicles transporting explosives must carry two fire extinguishers; school buses, public passenger vehicles and limited passenger vehicles seating more than 10 must carry one.

check.q: By how much does correct use of a lap and shoulder belt system reduce the likelihood of death in a crash?
check.explanation: Correct lap and shoulder belt use is estimated to reduce the likelihood of death in a crash by 50 per cent.

check.q: How many fire extinguishers must a vehicle transporting explosives carry?
check.explanation: Vehicles transporting explosives must carry two fire extinguishers.

summary: Keep a two-second following distance in taxis, limousines, ambulances or vans, and at least five seconds in buses and trucks.
Slow down to shrink your danger zone, cover the brake near hazards, and allow for off track in every turn.
Back up only when necessary: use a guide, sound your horn each vehicle length, and back to the view side.
Know the exam numbers: 60 m between big rigs, 70/40 km/h past flashing lights, 5-15 m railway stop, 30 m warning devices, 150 m headlight dimming.
Protect yourself: wear your seatbelt, avoid hand-held devices, never drive impaired or fatigued, and carry the required fire extinguishers.
